title: Job autonomy mattered for employment during the pandemic and for the occupations within workers’ reach
summary: Workers who started in occupations with more control over how they worked were more likely to be employed a year later during the pandemic, particularly in 2020. Julie Hotchkiss and M. Melinda Pitts find little evidence of that relationship either before or after the pandemic. Yet workers who remained employed showed no clear change across the three periods in how the quality of different occupations related to their decision to switch. Separating those outcomes changes the interpretation of the pandemic labour market. A temporary change in who could keep working can alter the mix of jobs without a lasting change in what workers want from a job.

The authors match workers in the Current Population Survey to interviews twelve months apart, obtaining about 1.6 million person-month observations. Every matched worker was employed at the first date. The share also employed at the second date was 91.3 percent before the pandemic, 89.1 percent from March 2020 through December 2022 and 91.2 percent from January 2023 through March 2025. Among people working at both endpoints, roughly 29 to 30 percent had a validated occupation change in each period. A person can be out of work between interviews or change employers without changing occupation. Neither outcome measures uninterrupted tenure with a particular employer.

To describe work, the authors combine employer information from the Occupational Requirements Survey with occupational information from O*NET. They construct autonomy and safety scores for 474 occupations. Control over pace, breaks and working position contributes to autonomy. The safety measure captures aspects of exposure, including contact with others. The scores stay fixed over time. The appendix explains why the underlying surveys are better suited to comparing occupations than to identifying changes within a job. A restaurant worker’s actual exposure could change during the pandemic even though the score attached to that occupation did not.

Which alternatives are within reach also matters. The authors infer plausible destinations from the occupations entered by other workers who leave the same starting occupation. In one comparison, an interquartile increase in destination autonomy was associated with a 7.4 percentage point rise in the probability of switching occupations. Estimates for the autonomy of the original job were smaller and less precise when destination quality was held fixed. The two characteristics are correlated, and their estimated effects could not be distinguished statistically. Available destination safety did not show a significant pull in the comparable specification. Higher pay in the occupation held tended to retain workers.

Workers who switched gained slightly more autonomy after March 2020 than previously, and slightly more safety after 2022. Those differences were small. The employment result offers a different possible mechanism for larger changes in aggregate job quality. Industries and occupations offering greater autonomy could have retained more workers when restrictions were most disruptive. The estimates also account for state policies and labour demand, but observed occupation changes still reflect employer demand, feasible alternatives and measurement error as well as preferences. An employer deciding whether to redesign a job should therefore consider the conditions at the jobs its workers can realistically take, while recognising that a survey match cannot tell whether a particular worker left voluntarily.

questions.question: Did greater autonomy protect employment through control over tasks, through the ability to work remotely, or through employer demand?
questions.detail: Compare employers facing similar demand shocks within occupations that differ in how much discretion workers actually have. Track remote-working arrangements and hours separately from the occupation-level score. The static scores cannot identify a workplace redesign during 2020, so additional within-occupation evidence could materially change the interpretation.

questions.question: How much does the 7.4 percentage point destination association describe workers’ choices rather than the offers they received?
questions.detail: Track applications, offers and vacancies in realistic destination occupations, including offers declined. A transition-based measure reflects where other workers successfully went, which depends on recruitment and credentials as well as preferences. Comparing similarly qualified workers with different local openings could help separate the attraction of autonomy from the availability of jobs.

questions.question: Who disappears from the analysis when a worker changes address or misses a survey interview?
questions.detail: The survey follows addresses, and response declined during the pandemic. Compare patterns using administrative employment records or a panel that follows movers. Check whether switchers with care responsibilities, insecure jobs or unusually large wage changes have different match rates. Stable patterns among matched respondents may coexist with a different experience for workers missing from the year-apart comparison.

limitation: The unit is a matched person-month, and the estimates describe the matched sample. Fixed occupational scores cannot measure a change in working conditions within an occupation.
